entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Dnieper–Carpathian Offensive was a pivotal military campaign fought during World War II. It took place in Right-bank Ukraine from December 24, 1943, to April 14, 1944, and was a crucial turning point in the war on the Eastern Front. The campaign involved a massive Soviet push against the German forces, who had occupied Ukraine since 1941. The Soviet victory marked a significant shift in the balance of power in the region.

The offensive was led by the Soviet commander, Fyodor Tolbukhin, and involved a series of battles, including the Battle of Nikopol, the Battle of Znamenka, and the Battle of Korsun-Shevchenkovsky. The campaign resulted in the defeat of the German 6th and 8th Armies and the capture of over 100,000 German soldiers.

The Dnieper–Carpathian Offensive had far-reaching consequences, shaping the course of World War II and the post-war world order. It paved the way for the Soviet occupation of Eastern Europe and the division of Europe into Eastern and Western blocs.

The campaign also had a profound impact on the Ukrainian people, who suffered greatly during the war. The Soviet victory marked a turning point in the struggle for Ukrainian independence and sovereignty.

In the end, the Dnieper–Carpathian Offensive was a testament to the bravery and sacrifice of the Soviet soldiers, who fought against overwhelming odds to secure a crucial victory for the Soviet Union.

The campaign also had a lasting impact on the world, shaping the course of international relations and the global balance of power. It demonstrated the power and resilience of the Soviet Union, which would go on to play a dominant role in world affairs for decades to come.

As one historian noted, 'The Dnieper–Carpathian Offensive was a turning point in the war, marking the beginning of the end of German dominance in the region.'
